cues.text: Chapter four: warehouses, lakes and modern data platforms.
Let's begin with the vocabulary, because these terms are easy to blur together.
OLTP stands for online transaction processing.
It handles frequent, short transactions and writes.
Think of recording a payment or updating an account balance.
OLAP, online analytical processing, is different.
It handles aggregations over substantial historical data, such as totals across months or years.
Now the storage platforms.
A data warehouse integrates cleaned, structured, historical data, and it is optimised for analytics.
A data lake stores diverse data, both raw and curated formats, often in object storage.
A lakehouse combines lake storage with table metadata, transactional features and governance.
A data mart focuses on one particular business area.
And a federated database queries autonomous sources without necessarily centralising all the data in one place.
Next, a table comparing warehouse and lake across four dimensions.
The columns are Dimension, Warehouse, and Lake.
First row, schema.
A warehouse is usually schema-on-write, meaning the structure is defined before data is stored.
A lake is often schema-on-read, meaning structure is applied when the data is read.
Second row, data.
A warehouse holds curated, structured data.
A lake holds raw and diverse data.
Third row, users.
A warehouse serves business intelligence and reporting users.
A lake serves engineering, data science and analytics users.
Fourth row, risks.
A warehouse risks rigid models and load delay.
A lake risks poor cataloguing and poor quality, which turns it into what is called a data swamp.
Now, how does data get into these systems?
ETL extracts, transforms, then loads.
ELT extracts, loads, then transforms on the target platform.
The only difference is where and when the transformation happens.
Change data capture, or CDC, streams changes from the source.
To work well, it needs ordering, schema evolution, recovery and reconciliation.
Then there is modelling.
A star schema has a central fact table holding measures, surrounded by dimension tables holding descriptive attributes.
A snowflake schema normalises those dimensions further.
One rule to remember: define the fact grain before designing the measures.
The grain says what exactly one row represents.
Here is an example.
A sales fact table has one row per order item.
It references the Date, Product and Store dimensions, and it stores quantity and revenue.
To analyse it, group revenue by region and month.
Two cautions: do not join two fact tables at incompatible grains, and do not double count sales.
Now the SQL query.
The source does not say it was executed, so treat it as an illustration of the pattern.
The SELECT clause returns the month from the date dimension, the region from the store dimension, and the sum of revenue from the fact table, labelled total.
The FROM clause starts at fact_sales, aliased as f.
The first JOIN links dim_date, aliased d, to the fact table where the date_id values match.
The second JOIN links dim_store, aliased s, where the store_id values match.
Finally, GROUP BY month and region means one result row per month and region combination, each with its summed revenue.
This is exactly the grouping of revenue by region and month described a moment ago.
Last, storage mechanics.
Columnar analytical storage reads selected columns efficiently.
Compression and partition pruning reduce I/O.
And lakehouse table formats such as Delta and Iceberg support metadata, versioning and updates, according to the implementation.
